meta.note: the constellations' spoken lines; recorded as voice/<lang>/<key>.mp3 when voice/manifest.json lists them

con_and.t: I am Andromeda. Chained to a sea rock for my mother’s boast, I waited for the monster. Perseus came, and now I shine beside him.

con_aqr.t: I am Ganymede, the Trojan boy Zeus carried up to Olympus. I pour the gods’ drink, and my water flows down to the Southern Fish.

con_aql.t: I am the eagle of Zeus. I carry his thunderbolts, and once I carried the boy Ganymede up to Olympus.

con_ara.t: I am Hestia. On this altar the gods swore their oath before the war with the Titans; its smoke rises as the Milky Way.

con_ari.t: I am the golden ram. I carried Phrixus over the sea to Colchis, and my fleece, hung in a sacred grove, called Jason’s Argo.

con_aur.t: I am Erichthonius of Athens, who first yoked four horses to a chariot. In my arms rides the goat Amalthea, who nursed the infant Zeus.

con_boo.t: I am Boötes, the herdsman. I drive the two Bears around the pole, and Arcturus, the guardian of the Bear, shines at my knee.

con_cnc.t: I am Hera. When Heracles fought my Hydra, I sent this crab to nip his foot. He crushed it; I set it among the stars.

con_cma.t: I am Orion’s great hound. In my jaw burns Sirius, the scorching one: when it rose with the Sun, the dog days began.

con_cmi.t: I am Orion’s lesser dog. My star is Procyon, “before the dog”: it rises just ahead of Sirius, the great hound’s star.

con_cap.t: I am Pan. When the monster Typhon fell upon the gods, I leapt into the river and changed: a goat above, a fish below.

con_cas.t: I am Cassiopeia, queen of Ethiopia. I boasted that I was lovelier than the sea nymphs; Poseidon set me on a throne turning upside down.

con_cen.t: I am Chiron, the wise centaur, teacher of Achilles and Asclepius. Wounded by a poisoned arrow, I gave up my immortality and came here.

con_cep.t: I am Cepheus, king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia. To save my kingdom from the sea monster, I chained our daughter Andromeda to the rock.

con_cet.t: I am Poseidon. I sent this sea monster against Ethiopia, for Cassiopeia’s boast. Perseus killed it before it could reach Andromeda.

con_cra.t: I am Dionysus. I brought my mother Semele up from the underworld, and set this wreath among the stars in her honour.

con_crb.t: I am Ariadne. Theseus left me on Naxos; Dionysus found me and married me, and threw my wedding crown up among the stars.

con_crv.t: I am Apollo. I sent my raven for water; he dawdled and lied to me. Now he sits beside the Cup, forever thirsty.

con_crt.t: I am Apollo’s raven. This is the cup I was sent to fill. The Water Snake guards it, and I can never drink.

con_cyg.t: I am Zeus. I came to Leda as a swan. Now my wings stretch along the Milky Way, and Deneb burns in my tail.

con_del.t: I am the dolphin who found Amphitrite hiding in the sea and brought her to Poseidon as his bride. In thanks he set me here.

con_dra.t: I am Ladon, the serpent who never slept, guarding the golden apples of the Hesperides. Heracles killed me; I coil forever around the pole.

con_equ.t: I am the little horse, only my head showing, running just ahead of Pegasus. I am the second smallest of all the constellations.

con_eri.t: I am Helios. My son Phaethon drove my chariot and lost the reins. Zeus struck him down, and he fell into this river, Eridanus.

con_gem.t: I am Polydeuces. When my mortal twin Castor died, I shared my immortality with him. Now we are never parted.

con_her.t: I am Heracles, son of Zeus. I finished my twelve labours, and here I kneel, my foot on the dragon’s head.

con_hya.t: I am the Hydra of Lerna. For every head Heracles cut off, two grew back, until fire sealed the wounds. I am the longest constellation.

con_leo.t: I am the lion of Nemea. No weapon could pierce my skin; Heracles strangled me with his bare hands and wore me as his cloak.

con_lep.t: I am the hare at Orion’s feet. The hunter’s dogs chase me across the sky every night, and they never catch me.

con_lib.t: I am Dike, Justice, daughter of Zeus. These are my scales. The Greeks first saw them as the Scorpion’s claws.

con_lup.t: I am the beast the Centaur carries to the Altar as an offering. The Greeks called me simply Therion, the beast; the Romans, the wolf.

con_lyr.t: I am Orpheus. With this lyre, which Hermes made from a tortoise shell, I charmed the rocks and the lord of the dead.

con_oph.t: I am Asclepius, the healer. I learned to bring the dead back to life; Zeus struck me down, then set me here, holding the serpent.

con_ori.t: I am Orion, the hunter. I boasted I would kill every beast on earth; a scorpion stung me. Now I set as the Scorpion rises.

con_peg.t: I am Pegasus, the winged horse, born from Medusa’s blood. Where my hoof struck Mount Helicon, the spring of the Muses welled up.

con_per.t: I am Perseus. I cut off Medusa’s head and freed Andromeda from the sea monster. Algol, the demon star, is Medusa’s winking eye.

con_psc.t: I am Aphrodite. When Typhon attacked the gods, my son Eros and I became two fishes and swam away, tied together by a cord.

con_psa.t: I am the Southern Fish. I drink the water Aquarius pours, and Fomalhaut, my mouth, shines alone in the autumn sky.

con_sge.t: I am Prometheus. Every day the eagle of Zeus tore at me, until Heracles shot it with this arrow and set me free.

con_sgr.t: I am Crotus, who lived among the Muses and invented the bow. My arrow points at the Scorpion’s heart, red Antares.

con_sco.t: I am Gaia, Mother Earth. When Orion boasted he would kill every creature, I sent this scorpion. The two never share the sky.

con_ser.t: I am the serpent that showed Asclepius the healing herb. He holds me still: my head on one side, my tail on the other.

con_tau.t: I am Europa. Zeus came to me as a gentle white bull; I climbed onto his back, and he swam with me to Crete.

con_tri.t: I am Hermes. I set this triangle above the faint Ram, so it could be found. The Greeks called it Deltoton, after the letter delta.

con_uma.t: I am Callisto. Zeus loved me; jealous Hera turned me into a bear. Zeus set me in the sky, circling the pole, never setting.

con_umi.t: I am Arcas, Callisto’s son. Hunting, I almost killed my mother, a bear. Zeus set us both in the sky; my tail holds Polaris.

con_vir.t: I am Demeter. My daughter Persephone holds the ear of wheat, Spica. While she is below, the fields sleep; when she returns, they grow.

con_argo.t: I am Athena. I helped build the Argo for Jason and his heroes. Now its keel, its stern and its sails cross the southern sky.

con_ant.t: Antlia, the air pump: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the instruments of science he set among the southern stars.

con_aps.t: Apus, the bird of paradise: charted by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_cae.t: Caelum, the engraver’s chisel: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the tools he set among the faint southern stars.

con_cam.t: Camelopardalis, the giraffe: drawn by Petrus Plancius in 1612 to fill an empty stretch of the northern sky.

con_cvn.t: Canes Venatici, the hunting dogs that Boötes holds on a leash: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1687.

con_cha.t: Chamaeleon: charted by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_cir.t: Circinus, the drawing compasses: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, beside the Southern Triangle and the Set Square.

con_col.t: Columba, Noah’s dove with the olive branch: drawn by Petrus Plancius in 1592 from stars south of the Hare.

con_com.t: Coma Berenices, Queen Berenice’s hair: named by the astronomer Conon in about 245 BC, and made a constellation by Vopel in 1536.

con_cru.t: Crux, the Southern Cross, the smallest constellation: once the Centaur’s feet, drawn apart by navigators in the 1590s and fixed by Royer in 1679.

con_dor.t: Dorado, the dolphinfish: charted by Keyser and de Houtman, on Plancius’s globe of 1598. The Large Magellanic Cloud lies within it.

con_for.t: Fornax, the chemical furnace: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the instruments of science he set among the southern stars.

con_gru.t: Grus, the crane: charted by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_hor.t: Horologium, the pendulum clock: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, in honour of the clocks that time the stars.

con_hyi.t: Hydrus, the little water snake of the south: charted by Keyser and de Houtman, on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_ind.t: Indus, the Indian: charted by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_lac.t: Lacerta, the lizard: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1687, a small zigzag of stars between the Swan and Andromeda.

con_lmi.t: Leo Minor, the little lion: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1687, from faint stars above the Lion’s back.

con_lyn.t: Lynx: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1687. Its stars are so faint, he said, that you need the eyes of a lynx to see them.

con_men.t: Mensa, Table Mountain: named by Lacaille in the 1750s after the mountain above Cape Town, where he charted the southern stars.

con_mic.t: Microscopium, the microscope: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the instruments of science he set among the southern stars.

con_mon.t: Monoceros, the unicorn: drawn by Petrus Plancius in 1612, between Orion’s two dogs, across the winter Milky Way.

con_mus.t: Musca, the fly: charted by Keyser and de Houtman and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598 as a bee; Lacaille made it a fly.

con_nor.t: Norma, the carpenter’s set square: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the instruments he set among the southern stars.

con_oct.t: Octans, the octant, a navigator’s instrument: named by Lacaille in the 1750s. The south celestial pole lies within it.

con_pav.t: Pavo, the peacock: charted by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_phe.t: Phoenix, the bird that rises from its own ashes: charted by Keyser and de Houtman, on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_pic.t: Pictor, the painter’s easel: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the tools of the arts he set in the southern sky.

con_pyx.t: Pyxis, the mariner’s compass: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, from stars beside the old ship Argo.

con_ret.t: Reticulum, the little net: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, after the crosshairs of the telescope he measured stars with.

con_scl.t: Sculptor, the sculptor’s workshop: named by Lacaille in the 1750s. The south galactic pole lies within it.

con_sct.t: Scutum, the shield: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1684 for King Jan III Sobieski of Poland, the victor at Vienna.

con_sex.t: Sextans, the sextant: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1687, in memory of his own sextant, lost when his observatory burned.

con_tel.t: Telescopium, the telescope: named by Lacaille in the 1750s, one of the instruments of science he set among the southern stars.

con_tra.t: Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle: first drawn by Petrus Plancius in 1589, and given its name by Johann Bayer in 1603.

con_tuc.t: Tucana, the toucan: charted by Keyser and de Houtman, on Plancius’s globe of 1598. The Small Magellanic Cloud lies within it.

con_vol.t: Volans, the flying fish: charted by the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman, and drawn on Plancius’s globe of 1598.

con_vul.t: Vulpecula, the little fox, with a goose in its jaws: named by Johannes Hevelius in 1687.
